children.note: The consent banner and the footer's consent control are drawn on one condition (SC-030; proposed, for founder approval at contract review): the site runs an integration that needs consent, which is a consent category in use (a fixture's site.consent.categories is not empty), and on Salt for WordPress a WP Consent API plugin is also wired (wp_has_consent exists). Without one, WordPress keeps every integration that needs consent denied, failing closed as salt_consent() does, and draws neither. Salt for Next.js's own consent store is always wired, so its condition is the integration alone. A wired mechanism with no category in use draws neither: a visitor has nothing to choose. The banner (page.json) is drawn on the same condition. When it does not hold, the footer draws neither the control nor its status line. A fixture's site.consent says a mechanism is wired, and its categories are the ones in use.

notes.text: Footer links are drawn in columns. A single flat menu, as WordPress has, maps to one untitled column (SC-006): no title paragraph, and its list takes the nav's name.

The consent panel groups its boxes by WP Consent API category (SC-030). Each Salt category maps to one API category: analytics to statistics, embeds to marketing, marketing to marketing, and maps (Salt for WordPress's own category) to marketing; necessary is never a box. The panel draws one box per API category that at least one of the site's integrations uses, in the API's order, and only an API category some Salt category maps to can be one: statistics, then marketing. functional and preferences have no Salt category, so no box. statistics-anonymous is never drawn: Salt writes it with the statistics box's verdict, so a plugin that reads it agrees with the visitor's one choice. A wired mechanism with no category in use draws no control, no banner and no panel (proposed, for founder approval at contract review). The box's id, name and <category> are the API category; its label and description are the site's. Ticking a box grants every Salt category in its group, and clearing it refuses them all, so a visitor's choice reads the same through the WP Consent API (wp_has_consent) and through Salt's own gate, and no two boxes ever share one setting. A site whose integrations use only analytics draws one box, statistics.
Base order: text, social, theme toggle, display preferences, copyright, consent. WordPress today: social, text, copyright, preferences.

Every id the footer draws is fixed (SC-012), with the footer's own id as its owner, as sections.json names it: the consent panel is drawn by the footer, and the vocabulary has no consent component of its own. A column title is site-footer__column-<n>, <n> its column's position among the columns with links, counting from 1. The consent panel's title is site-footer__consent-title, and each category's checkbox and description are site-footer__consent-<category> and site-footer__consent-<category>-description, <category> the box's WP Consent API category (statistics, marketing). A drawn id contains __, which no anchor can, so none can meet an editor's anchor.

The consent panel's boxes by WP Consent API category (SC-030): one statistics box for analytics and one marketing box for embeds and marketing, named and id'd by the API category, each setting every Salt category in its group, in place of one box per Salt category (analytics, embeds, marketing).
